lesson.menu_title: Milestone -- The Simulated US Interview: The Questions You Ask Back
lesson.menu_desc: A full final round for an AI safety role, and the five minutes that decide it: the indirect question that lets an executive ask anything without sounding blunt -- word order, whether, and the do that disappears -- 32 slides
lesson.subtitle: Lesson 19 -- Milestone: The Simulated US Interview
lesson.title_tag: Professor View -- Lucia Nishiyama Serra | Lesson 19 -- Milestone: The Simulated US Interview

listenings.text: Hi, it is Dana. I am leaving this as a voice note before Thursday so you have it in writing from me as well. Here is how the final round works on our side. Four blocks, three hours with the break, and each block belongs to a different person with a different job. Marcus goes last and he is the one who decides. The first block is technical depth, the second one is the failed program, the third is the peer block, and that one is not a formality, because if that person says no we do not move. Two things I tell every candidate at your level and almost none of them believe me the first time. The first is that the peer block counts as much as the block with Marcus. The second is that the last ten minutes of the final block, when he asks whether you have questions, is not the polite part at the end. It is a block of its own, and he grades it. Bring four questions, not one, and do not spend them on things you could have found on our website. Ask about the reporting line, ask what the first year looks like, ask about the things that would make this role hard. And one small warning about compensation. Do not open that on Thursday. Bring it to me on Friday, that is what I am for, and Marcus will think better of you for it.

I want to talk about the last five minutes, because that is where I see senior people give away a job they had already won. The interviewer says, do you have any questions for me. And the candidate, who has been sharp for fifty minutes, says no, I think you covered everything. That sentence costs more than any answer in the hour. What the interviewer hears is that you were auditioning rather than deciding, and nobody senior is only auditioning. Now, how you ask matters as much as what you ask. A direct question in that moment can land hard. Who does this role report to sounds like an interrogation, and how much does it pay sounds like the end of a negotiation you never started. Put a frame in front of it and the same question becomes a conversation. Could you tell me who the role reports to. I was wondering how you would measure success in the first year. Do you know whether this is a new headcount. Same information, completely different room. And notice what happens inside the sentence once the frame is there. The word order goes back to normal, subject before verb, and the little do or does at the front simply disappears. My last piece of advice is about the one question everybody wants to ask and nobody should ask first. Leave compensation to the recruiter. In an American process that is her job, not his, and asking him makes the whole hour look like it was about the number.

extra_audio.text: Dana called on Monday to tell me I was on the shortlist. She walked me through the hiring loop and warned me that the peer block was not a formality. On Thursday the onsite ran for three hours and Marcus probed the failed program for twenty minutes. When he asked whether I had questions, I asked about the reporting line and about what would make the first year hard. And on Friday I took compensation to Dana, because that conversation was never his.
